questions.stem: What distinguishes an intelligent system from ordinary automation?
options: It gathers its data through sensors rather than relying on manual entry
It processes data in real time rather than on a fixed schedule
It applies a set of rules rather than executing a fixed sequence of steps
It has a feedback loop — it observes the outcome of its own decision and adjusts
questions.explanation: The feedback loop is the defining feature — (A), (B) and (C) all describe sophisticated automation that still never learns from its own results. Generic architecture: input (sensors/data) → processing → knowledge store → decision → output → feedback back into the knowledge store.

questions.stem: An intelligent agent is best defined as something that:
options: Executes a defined sequence of tasks on a user's behalf without supervision
Perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators to achieve a goal
Learns a model from labelled data and applies it to new cases
Presents analysed data to a human so that they can decide what to do
questions.explanation: The perceive–act loop is the definition. (A) describes automation or RPA, (C) machine learning, and (D) a DSS — all adjacent, none of them the agent. Its properties are autonomy, reactivity, proactivity, social ability and adaptability.

questions.stem: A thermostat that switches heating on below 18 °C is best classified as:
options: A decision support system
An expert system
A machine learning system
A rule-based system
questions.explanation: Rule-based — Pre-coded IF-THEN logic, no training, no adaptation, total explainability. (B) is the closest — an expert system also uses IF-THEN rules, but it encodes a domain expert's reasoning across many rules with an inference engine, not a single threshold.

questions.stem: The principal weakness of a machine learning system compared with a rule-based system is:
options: It cannot be updated once it has been trained and deployed
It is often a black box — the reasoning behind a decision cannot readily be inspected
It requires all of its rules to be written out explicitly before training begins
It performs poorly on the large datasets that rule-based systems handle easily
questions.explanation: (C) is the reverse of the truth and is the reason ML was adopted in the first place. Opacity matters legally and ethically wherever a decision affects someone's job, loan or liberty — hence explainable AI (XAI), model cards, and mandated notice for automated decisions.

questions.stem: A DSS differs from an expert system because it:
options: Supports human judgement by analysing data and presenting results, rather than emulating an expert's reasoning
Emulates an expert's reasoning, whereas an expert system merely presents analysed data
Handles structured decisions only, whereas an expert system handles unstructured ones
Learns from historical outcomes, whereas an expert system applies fixed rules
questions.explanation: DSS supports; expert system emulates. (B) is that relationship inverted. A DSS's components are data management, model management and the user interface, sometimes with a knowledge component added.

questions.stem: Which is not a standard component of a DSS?
options: Database / data management
Actuator control subsystem
Model management
User interface / dialogue management
questions.explanation: Actuators belong to control systems and IoT. A DSS informs a human; it does not physically act on the world — which is precisely the boundary between supporting a decision and making one.

questions.stem: "Reorder stock automatically when quantity falls below 20 units" is which category of decision?
options: Structured
Semi-structured
Unstructured
Strategic
questions.explanation: Structured — Routine, repetitive, criteria fully known — therefore fully automatable, with humans monitoring only. Operational level. (D) names a management level rather than a decision category, which is a distinction worth keeping clear.

questions.stem: "Should we enter the New Zealand market?" is which category?
options: Operational
Semi-structured
Structured
Unstructured
questions.explanation: Unstructured — An effectively infinite set of possible considerations, novel and judgement-dominant. The system informs; the human decides. Strategic/executive level.

questions.stem: A loan system scores applications automatically and refers borderline cases to a manager. This is:
options: Unstructured
Structured
Semi-structured
Strategic
questions.explanation: Semi-structured — a specified finite set of instructions handles part of the decision, and human judgement resolves the remainder. Tactical/middle-management level. The referral of borderline cases is the tell: a fully structured decision would need no referral path at all.

questions.stem: Moving from structured to unstructured decisions, which statement is true?
options: Ambiguity increases, but the consequence of a single error falls as more people review it
Ambiguity increases, decision frequency increases, and the scope for automation increases
Ambiguity decreases, data becomes more internal, and the system shifts from informing to deciding
Ambiguity increases, data sources become more external and unstructured, and the system's role shifts from deciding to informing
questions.explanation: Going down the pyramid: automation ↑, frequency ↑, consequence of a single error ↓. Going up: ambiguity ↑, external and unstructured data ↑, and the system merely informs. (A) inverts the error-consequence relationship, which is exactly backwards — strategic mistakes are the expensive ones.

questions.stem: Which DSS feature lets a manager ask "what happens to profit if input costs rise 8%"?
options: Drill-down
What-if / sensitivity analysis
Goal seeking
Data validation
questions.explanation: (C) is the near-miss and runs the other way — goal seeking starts from a desired outcome and finds the input needed to reach it. Sensitivity analysis reveals which assumptions the outcome is most fragile to, often more valuable than the point estimate itself.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a DSS in agriculture?
options: A system combining soil-moisture sensor data, weather forecasts and crop models to recommend irrigation timing
An irrigation controller that opens a valve whenever soil moisture falls below a set threshold
A dashboard reporting each paddock's yield across the past five seasons
A spreadsheet model projecting next season's yield from historical averages
questions.explanation: Multiple data sources plus models plus a recommendation to a human decision-maker — the defining DSS pattern. (B) is rule-based control that acts without a human, (C) is descriptive reporting with no model, and (D) is a model with no live data integration.

questions.stem: The three syllabus-named components of an expert system are:
options: Knowledge base, inference engine, explanation facility
Knowledge base, working memory, user interface
Knowledge base, inference engine, user interface
Database, model management, user interface
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) each substitute a genuine supporting part for one of the three core components — working memory holds the facts about this case, and the explanation facility traces the reasoning. Both are worth naming for extra depth, neither is in the core three. (D) is a DSS.

questions.stem: The knowledge base of an expert system contains:
options: The facts specific to the case currently being reasoned about
Domain facts plus IF-THEN production rules, often with certainty factors
The algorithm deciding which rules to apply, and in what order
The record of which rules fired, used to explain the conclusion
questions.explanation: Each distractor is the contents of a different component: (A) is working memory, (C) is the inference engine, and (D) is the explanation facility. The knowledge base holds what is true in general; working memory holds what is true now.

questions.stem: A knowledge engineer:
options: Designs and tunes the inference engine's rule-selection strategy
Interviews domain experts and encodes their knowledge as facts and rules
Curates and labels the training data used to fit a model
Maintains the servers and databases on which the system runs
questions.explanation: This is also the source of the knowledge acquisition bottleneck — experts routinely cannot articulate tacit knowledge they apply unconsciously, so the engineer must elicit it through cases and counter-examples rather than by asking directly.

questions.stem: Forward chaining is best described as:
options: Goal-driven — starting from a hypothesis and seeking the facts that would support it
Data-driven — starting from known facts and firing rules until a conclusion emerges
Probabilistic — weighting each rule by its certainty factor before deciding which to fire
Exhaustive — firing every rule in the knowledge base and reporting all resulting conclusions
questions.explanation: (A) is backward chaining. Memory hook: forward chaining is a sensor watching the world and working out what follows; backward chaining is a doctor with a hypothesis, asking you targeted questions.

questions.stem: A fault-diagnosis system that repeatedly asks the user targeted questions is most likely using:
options: Forward chaining
Backward chaining
Clustering
Ontology classification
questions.explanation: Backward chaining — It starts from a hypothesis and asks only for the facts needed to prove or disprove it — efficient when data is expensive to gather and the set of possible conclusions is small. The asking is the tell: forward chaining consumes facts it is given.

questions.stem: Real-time process monitoring with alarm generation is best served by:
options: Forward chaining, because data arrives continuously and the system must determine what it implies
Backward chaining, because it minimises the number of facts that must be gathered
Backward chaining, because an alarm condition is a hypothesis to be proved or disproved
Either, since the chaining strategy does not affect monitoring performance
questions.explanation: (C) is the sophisticated trap — you could frame an alarm as a hypothesis, but there is nobody to ask, and the system would have to test every possible alarm continuously. Data arrives from sensors unbidden, so the system must derive consequences as facts accumulate.

questions.stem: The explanation facility is important because it:
options: Traces the rule chain so the user can see why a conclusion was reached, making the system trustworthy and legally defensible
Records which rules fired, so the knowledge engineer can debug the knowledge base
Translates the system's technical output into language a non-expert can understand
Documents the source from which each rule in the knowledge base was derived
questions.explanation: (B) is a genuine by-product — the same trace serves debugging — but the facility exists for the user, not the developer. It answers "why are you asking this?" and "how did you reach that conclusion?", a capability most modern black-box ML systems lack.

questions.stem: Rules R1 (CF 1.0) → R2 (CF 0.8) → R3 (CF 0.6) fire in a chain. The conclusion's confidence is:
questions.explanation: 0.48 — Multiply along the chain: 1.0 × 0.8 × 0.6 = 0.48. (D) is what you get by applying the combining formula for independent evidence — the wrong rule for a chain. Confidence decays down a long chain, which is why the system should report "moderate confidence, seek more evidence" rather than assert a diagnosis.

questions.stem: Two independent rules support the same conclusion with CF 0.6 and CF 0.5. Using CF = CF1 + CF2(1 − CF1), the combined confidence is:
questions.explanation: 0.80 — 0.6 + 0.5(1 − 0.6) = 0.6 + 0.2 = 0.8. Each wrong option is a specific error: (B) averages, (C) multiplies as if the rules were chained, and (A) simply adds. Independent supporting evidence raises confidence without ever exceeding 1.

questions.stem: MYCIN is a classic example of an expert system used for:
options: Medical diagnosis of blood infections
Configuring minicomputer systems to order
Mineral exploration and prospecting
Scheduling airline crew rosters
questions.explanation: (B) is XCON, which configured DEC computers, and (C) is PROSPECTOR — both are real systems from the same era, so the names have to be learned rather than guessed. MYCIN is the canonical diagnosis example and pioneered certainty factors.

questions.stem: Which is not one of the four syllabus applications of expert systems?
options: Process control
Diagnosis
Monitoring
Data warehousing
questions.explanation: The four are diagnosis, monitoring, process control, and scheduling/planning. Interpretation, design/configuration and instruction are commonly added for extra depth.

questions.stem: The knowledge acquisition bottleneck refers to:
options: The time the inference engine takes to search a very large rule set
The shortage of labelled training data available to fit a model
The difficulty of extracting and formalising expert knowledge, especially tacit knowledge experts cannot articulate
The difficulty of keeping the knowledge base current as the domain itself changes
questions.explanation: (D) is the closest — knowledge maintenance is a genuine and separate problem, and it is why expert systems age badly. The bottleneck is at the point of acquisition: it is the main reason expert systems are slow and expensive to build, and a major driver of the shift toward learning from data instead.

questions.stem: A significant risk of an expert system operating outside its narrow domain is:
options: It reports a low certainty factor, correctly signalling that the case is out of scope
It refuses to reach a conclusion, since no rule in its knowledge base matches the input
It fails badly and, lacking common sense, does not recognise that it is failing
It degrades gradually in accuracy as unfamiliar cases accumulate
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) describe what people assume will happen, and it is the assumption that makes the risk dangerous — a rule set can fire confidently on inputs it was never designed for and return a fully certain wrong answer. Brittleness plus false confidence is the lethal combination; human oversight and explicit scope boundaries are the controls.

questions.stem: Which factor did not drive the shift from purely rule-based to probabilistic expert systems?
options: Greater availability of and access to data
Increased processing power
The decline of the internet
Falling hardware costs
questions.explanation: The syllabus factors are processing power, data availability and access, hardware costs, neural networks and webometrics — the internet's growth was an enabler of the shift, not a decline.

questions.stem: Webometrics contributes to intelligent systems by:
options: Indexing web pages so that a search engine can retrieve them by keyword
Monitoring the performance and uptime of an enterprise's web servers
Measuring how long users spend on each page, in order to improve site design
Quantitatively measuring web content, links, usage and citations, giving statistical evidence of relevance and authority
questions.explanation: Link analysis behind PageRank is the classic example — authority inferred statistically from the structure of the web, rather than hand-coded by experts. (A) is indexing, which is what makes retrieval possible; webometrics is what makes ranking possible.

questions.stem: Which inference technique automatically withdraws conclusions when a supporting premise is retracted?
options: Ontology classification
Hypothetical reasoning
Fuzzy logic
Truth maintenance
questions.explanation: Truth maintenance — It records the justification for every derived fact, keeping the knowledge base consistent and supporting non-monotonic reasoning — essential where symptoms or evidence get revised. (B) is the near-miss: hypothetical reasoning entertains assumptions without committing, but does not retract on your behalf.

questions.stem: A washing machine that adjusts its cycle for a load described as "slightly soiled" is using:
options: Fuzzy logic
Certainty factors
Heuristic knowledge
Truth maintenance
questions.explanation: Fuzzy logic — degrees of truth between 0 and 1, handling linguistic variables through membership functions. (B) is the sharpest distractor: both express something other than binary truth, but a certainty factor expresses confidence in a conclusion, whereas fuzzy logic expresses degree of membership in a category. Also used in camera autofocus, ABS braking, HVAC and medical dosing.

questions.stem: Heuristic knowledge in an inference engine provides:
options: Rules guaranteed to find the optimal solution, given sufficient time
Rules of thumb that give a good-enough answer quickly by pruning the search space
Rules expressing degrees of membership rather than binary truth
Rules recording the justification for each fact the system has derived
questions.explanation: Used where exhaustive search is impossible — chess engines, A route-finding, scheduling. (A) inverts the defining trade-off: a heuristic buys speed by giving up* the guarantee of optimality. (C) is fuzzy logic and (D) truth maintenance.

questions.stem: Ontology classification enables an inference engine to:
options: Measure the uncertainty attached to each conclusion it derives
Assign each new case to the group whose existing members it most closely resembles
Reason about categories and inherit properties through formal is-a and part-of hierarchies
Retract a conclusion once the fact supporting it has been withdrawn
questions.explanation: (B) is clustering, and the distinction is worth holding onto: an ontology's categories are defined in advance by humans with formal relationships, whereas clusters are discovered from the data. Ontologies sit behind the semantic web, biomedical vocabularies (SNOMED, Gene Ontology) and the knowledge graphs powering search assistants.

questions.stem: Hypothetical reasoning is best illustrated by:
options: Assigning a confidence value to each conclusion and combining them as evidence accumulates
Starting from one hypothesis and asking only for the facts needed to confirm or refute it
Assuming each of several competing diagnoses is true in turn and exploring the consequences, without committing to any
Withdrawing a conclusion automatically once its supporting premise is retracted
questions.explanation: (B) is backward chaining — an excellent near-miss, since both begin from a hypothesis. The difference is plurality and commitment: backward chaining pursues one goal to a verdict, while hypothetical reasoning holds several possible worlds open at once. Used in medical differential diagnosis, financial scenario analysis and forensic reasoning.

questions.stem: The Internet of Me (IoMe) is best described as:
options: A framework granting individuals legal ownership of the data their devices generate
A public IoT network operated and regulated by government
A protocol allowing personal devices to communicate without a central hub
The personalised, individual-centred layer of IoT built around one person's data and context
questions.explanation: Wearables, health apps, assistants, personalised feeds, adaptive homes. (A) is the poignant distractor — the IoMe is precisely what makes that framework necessary, since it concentrates deeply intimate data (heart rate, sleep, location, mood) in commercial hands.

questions.stem: Industry 4.0 is characterised by:
options: Electronics, computers and programmable automation applied to the production line
Cyber-physical systems, IIoT, big data, AI, robotics and digital twins producing self-optimising smart factories
Electricity and mass production on the moving assembly line
Human–machine collaboration, mass personalisation and sustainability
questions.explanation: (A) is the third revolution and (C) the second — but (D) is the real trap: that is Industry 5.0, the successor concept, so the answer depends on knowing where 4.0 ends. 1st = steam and mechanisation, 4th = connected intelligence.

questions.stem: A web crawler that follows links, respects robots.txt and passes pages to an indexer is:
options: A decision support system, since it supplies the data the ranking algorithm uses
A complex agent, since it must decide which links to follow next
An expert system, since it applies encoded rules to decide what to index
A simplistic agent — reactive, rule-following and non-learning
questions.explanation: (B) is tempting because "deciding" sounds sophisticated, but following links in a defined order according to fixed rules is reactive, not deliberative. The complex agents in a search engine are the ranking and understanding systems: semantic intent, personalisation, knowledge-graph reasoning and spam detection.

questions.stem: Predictive search strings (autocomplete) raise which significant social concern?
options: They prevent personalisation, since suggestions are drawn from aggregate behaviour
They reduce the accuracy of results by steering users away from their original query
They slow the search process, since users must read and dismiss the suggestions
They shape what people search for and consider normal, can surface offensive suggestions, and reveal that queries are logged
questions.explanation: Suggestion is not neutral — it is a nudge applied at enormous scale, and it simultaneously makes visible that every query is retained and aggregated. (B) and (C) treat a social problem as a usability one.

questions.stem: Order the voice assistant pipeline correctly:
options: Wake word → NLU → ASR → dialogue manager → action → response generation → TTS
Wake word → ASR → NLU → dialogue manager → action → response generation → TTS
ASR → wake word → NLU → dialogue manager → action → response generation → TTS
Wake word → ASR → dialogue manager → NLU → action → response generation → TTS
questions.explanation: All four contain the same stages, so the sequence is the whole question. Wake-word detection → speech-to-text → natural-language understanding (intent + entities) → dialogue manager → action/API call → response generation → text-to-speech. Note (A) would require understanding audio before transcribing it.

questions.stem: The most serious privacy concern with home voice assistants is:
options: Always-listening microphones in private spaces, with recordings retained and sometimes reviewed by humans
The assistant's failure to recognise all accents and dialects equally well
A single spoken answer removing the user's ability to compare competing sources
The requirement for a permanent connection to a commercial provider's servers
questions.explanation: (B) is a genuine equity concern and (C) a genuine epistemic one — both are real criticisms of voice assistants, and neither is a privacy concern, which is what the stem asks for. Human review of recordings is the detail most users do not expect.

questions.stem: An actuator in an intelligent system:
options: Converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal
Converts electrical signals into physical action
Converts a continuous signal into discrete digital values
Converts digital values into a continuous output signal
questions.explanation: Sensors are the senses — option (A) — and actuators are the muscles: servos, solenoids, relays, pumps, valves. (C) is an ADC and (D) a DAC, the two converters that sit between them and the processor.

questions.stem: An ADC is required because:
options: Continuous analog sensor signals must be converted into discrete digital values the processor can handle
Digital processor outputs must be converted into continuous signals that actuators can use
Sensor signals must be amplified before they are strong enough to be read reliably
Sensor readings must be timestamped so that their order can be reconstructed
questions.explanation: (B) is the DAC, which performs exactly the reverse — the two are easy to swap under pressure. Sampling rate and resolution determine how faithfully the original signal is captured.

questions.stem: Which is a biometric input?
options: An RFID access card read at a door
A gait or keystroke-dynamics recogniser
A PIN pad on a payment terminal
An ultrasonic proximity sensor
questions.explanation: Biometrics identify from unique physiological or behavioural traits — fingerprint, face, iris, voiceprint, palm vein, gait, typing rhythm. (A) is something you have and (C) something you know; only biometrics are something you are.

questions.stem: Edge processing is preferred over cloud processing when:
options: A model must be trained on data pooled from very many devices
Maximum available compute power and centrally managed updates matter most
Low latency, offline operation, bandwidth savings or keeping sensitive data local matter most
The data must be retained long-term for historical trend analysis
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (D) are all cases where the cloud wins. Edge wins on latency, resilience, bandwidth and privacy; cloud wins on raw compute, easier updates and cross-device learning. Most real architectures do both.

questions.stem: In computational thinking, abstraction applied to a self-driving car means:
options: Recognising that the same braking logic applies to cyclists and pedestrians
Splitting the system into perception, planning and control subsystems
Representing a pedestrian as a bounding box with a position and a velocity
Writing the step-by-step procedure the car follows at an intersection
questions.explanation: Abstraction strips away detail irrelevant to the decision. Each distractor is a different computational thinking component: (B) is decomposition, (A) pattern recognition, and (D) algorithm design — so all four options are correct descriptions of something, and only one matches the term.

questions.stem: In a flowchart, the diamond represents:
options: A decision
A process
Input/output
A terminator
questions.explanation: Decision — Oval = terminator, rectangle = process, parallelogram = input/output, cylinder = stored data. Every decision diamond must have exactly two labelled exits — an unlabelled branch is a common mark-losing error.

questions.stem: In a DFD, a data store may:
options: Exchange data only with a process
Connect directly to an external entity, provided the flow is labelled
Have inputs but no outputs, where the data is only being archived
Represent a person or organisation that supplies data to the system
questions.explanation: Data must flow via a process — something has to do the reading or writing. (C) is the "archive" excuse for a black hole, which is still an error; (D) describes an external entity. Store-to-store and entity-to-entity flows are likewise errors, as are miracles (output with no input).

questions.stem: A decision tree with certainty factors differs from a plain decision tree because:
options: Each leaf carries a confidence value, and the highest-confidence leaf is selected
Each branch carries a probability, and the probabilities along a path are summed
Each branch carries a confidence value, multiplied along a path to give the overall confidence
Each branch is weighted by how frequently it was taken in the training data
questions.explanation: Each root-to-leaf path is effectively an IF-THEN rule with an associated confidence, letting the system express graded rather than binary conclusions. (B) is the arithmetic error to avoid — confidences along a chain multiply, so they decay rather than accumulate.

questions.stem: Which diagram best communicates an intelligent system's purpose to a non-technical public audience?
options: A flowchart of the system's decision logic
A Level 0 context diagram
An infographic
A network topology diagram
questions.explanation: Infographic — icons, a linear narrative and minimal jargon. (B) is the strongest distractor: a context diagram is the most accessible of the technical models, since it hides all internal detail — but it still uses notation the public has never been taught to read.

questions.stem: MQTT is used in IoT networks because it is:
options: An encryption standard securing traffic between devices and the gateway
A lightweight request/response protocol for constrained devices, built on UDP
A lightweight publish/subscribe protocol suited to constrained devices and unreliable links
A long-range, low-power radio standard for battery-powered sensors
questions.explanation: (B) is CoAP, the genuine alternative — the distinction is publish/subscribe versus request/response. Pub/sub decouples devices from consumers and avoids the overhead of constant polling. (D) is LoRaWAN, a different layer of the stack entirely.

questions.stem: LoRaWAN / NB-IoT are chosen over Wi-Fi for:
options: Short-range links between a wearable and the phone it pairs with
High-bandwidth, low-latency links for machine vision on a production line
Long-range, low-power, low-data-rate sensor reporting, such as soil moisture across a farm
High-speed backhaul between a site's gateway and the cloud
questions.explanation: Range and battery life, bought at the cost of bandwidth — a LoRaWAN node can run for years on a battery and send a few bytes an hour. (A) is Bluetooth LE; 5G is the choice where high bandwidth and low latency are both required.

questions.stem: The primary role of an IoT gateway / edge node is to:
options: Provide devices with their network addresses and route their traffic to the internet
Aggregate, filter and pre-process device data, translate protocols, and make local decisions when latency matters
Hold the enterprise's historical sensor data for later analysis
Authenticate each device and issue it with the credentials it requires
questions.explanation: (A) describes a router — a gateway does route, but that is not what makes it a gateway rather than a switch. It is the point at which surplus data is removed before it consumes bandwidth and cloud storage.

questions.stem: Distinguishing relevant from surplus data in an IoT network matters because:
options: Surplus data degrades model accuracy by introducing noise into the training set
Filtering at the edge cuts bandwidth, storage and cost, and supports the obligation to collect only what is necessary
Surplus data must be encrypted to a higher standard, raising the processing overhead
Relevant data has to be retained for longer, so it must be identified at the point of capture
questions.explanation: The answer has both a cost and a privacy half, and a full-mark response names both. Strategies: edge filtering, event-driven reporting, aggregation, sampling and tiered retention.

questions.stem: Segmenting IoT devices onto their own VLAN primarily:
options: Allows all devices to be managed and updated from a single console
Increases the bandwidth available to each device
Reduces the power each device consumes while idle
Prevents a compromised device from reaching corporate systems
questions.explanation: IoT devices are frequently unpatched, weakly authenticated and impossible to run security software on, which makes them a favoured entry point. Segmentation contains the blast radius — the compromised camera can still be compromised, it just cannot reach the finance server.

questions.stem: Which correctly orders the IoT data lifecycle?
options: Storage → collection → transmission → processing → application → archive/deletion
Collection → application → transmission → storage → processing → archive/deletion
Collection → transmission → storage → processing → application → archive/deletion
Collection → archive/deletion → transmission → storage → processing → application
questions.explanation: The type of data (structured telemetry, semi-structured JSON, unstructured video) is determined at collection and shapes every later stage — which is why decisions made in the first step constrain everything downstream.

questions.stem: A digital twin is:
options: A live virtual replica, continuously fed by real sensor data from its physical counterpart
A detailed simulation model of a physical asset, built once from its design specification
A duplicate of the production system, kept synchronised and ready for failover
A complete historical record of a physical asset's sensor readings over its lifetime
questions.explanation: (B) is the sharpest distractor — a design-based simulation is a model, and what makes a twin a twin is the live data link to the specific physical instance, complete with its wear, faults and history. Used for monitoring, what-if testing and predictive maintenance: you experiment on the twin rather than on the running plant.

questions.stem: RPA (robotic process automation) automates:
options: Judgement-based tasks, by learning from how a human performs them
Physical robotic arms working on an assembly line
Routing and load-balancing decisions taken across a network
Rule-based back-office software tasks, such as re-entering data between two systems
questions.explanation: (A) is the standard misconception — RPA follows rules and does not learn. Combining it with AI ("intelligent automation") is what extends it to tasks requiring classification or extraction from unstructured documents.

questions.stem: Monte Carlo simulation is used in business analytics to:
options: Model risk by running many randomised scenarios to produce a distribution of possible outcomes
Produce a single best-estimate forecast by averaging a large number of historical observations
Identify which input assumption the outcome is most sensitive to, varying one at a time
Find the input value that would produce a specified target outcome
questions.explanation: (C) is sensitivity analysis and (D) is goal seeking — three distinct what-if techniques a DSS might offer. Monte Carlo's output is a probability distribution, not a point estimate, which makes it appropriate exactly when uncertainty is the thing you need to quantify.

questions.stem: Simulation is preferred for high-risk applications because:
options: Simulation removes the need for physical testing before the system is deployed
The consequences of real-world failure are catastrophic, so scenarios are modelled before commitment
Simulation eliminates the uncertainty inherent in the system being modelled
Regulators accept simulated results in place of operational evidence
questions.explanation: (A), (C) and (D) all overclaim in the specific way that makes simulation dangerous — it reduces the number of expensive real-world failures without ever replacing real-world validation. Applications: nuclear, aviation, autonomous vehicles, drug trials, bushfire and flood modelling. Requirements: validated models, redundancy, human oversight, clear accountability.

questions.stem: The core limitation of any simulation is:
options: Its results cannot be validated against real-world outcomes
It cannot incorporate real measured data, only estimated parameters
It requires computing power beyond the reach of most enterprises
It is only as good as its assumptions and inputs, and cannot capture genuine novelty
questions.explanation: Black swan events lie outside the modelled distribution by definition — a simulation can only explore the world you told it about. Over-confidence in a model's output is itself a risk factor, and arguably the one that has caused the most damage.

questions.stem: VR training simulators for mining or surgery are justified primarily because:
options: They remove the need for any supervised practice on live equipment
They cost substantially less to develop than conventional training materials
They close the fidelity gap between training conditions and real operating conditions
They allow safe, repeatable practice of dangerous or expensive scenarios, with objective performance measurement
questions.explanation: (A) and (C) are precisely the overclaims a balanced answer must reject — the fidelity gap is VR's central limitation, not something it eliminates. Other limitations worth naming: cost, motion sickness, and no substitute for real-world unpredictability.

questions.stem: The most significant and irreversible risk of biometric data compared with passwords is:
options: Biometrics are matched probabilistically, so a false match is always possible
Biometrics cannot be stored in an encrypted form
Biometrics cannot be revoked or reissued once they have been breached
Biometrics require specialised hardware that not every device provides
questions.explanation: (A) is a real and important limitation — but a false match can be re-tested, whereas you cannot get a new fingerprint. Biometric data is also classified as sensitive information under the Privacy Act, requiring explicit consent.

questions.stem: Documented demographic accuracy gaps in facial recognition mean:
options: Accuracy is determined chiefly by camera resolution and lighting rather than by the subject
False-match rates have been shown to be higher for darker-skinned and female faces, risking wrongful accusation
The gaps disappear once a system is trained on a sufficiently large dataset
The gaps affect verification (one-to-one) but not identification (one-to-many)
questions.explanation: (C) is the plausible-sounding falsehood worth being able to rebut: a very large dataset that remains unrepresentative reproduces the gap at scale, since size and representativeness are different properties. This is algorithmic bias with direct physical consequences, and is central to debates over retail and police deployment in Australia.

questions.stem: The strongest ethical concern about customer loyalty schemes is:
options: Non-members are charged a higher shelf price for identical goods
The discounts offered are worth less to the member than the scheme costs to administer
Loyalty data is retained indefinitely, which exceeds what the APPs permit
Consumers underestimate what they have traded, and purchase patterns can reveal inferred sensitive attributes such as pregnancy or illness
questions.explanation: Consent buried in terms and conditions, plus onward sharing and price discrimination, is the pattern to name. (A) is a real practice and a real fairness question — but it is a pricing issue, not the ethical problem of inference without consent.

questions.stem: ML fraud detection's principal cost to legitimate customers is:
options: False positives — legitimate transactions blocked, with opaque decisions and weak appeal rights
False negatives — fraudulent transactions approved, with the loss falling on the customer
Slower checkout, since every transaction must be scored before it is authorised
Higher fees, since the cost of running the detection system is passed on
questions.explanation: (B) is the sharpest near-miss: false negatives are a real cost, but they fall primarily on the bank, which typically reimburses. The remedy for false positives is a human review queue, transparency about the decision, and a genuine right of appeal — which maps directly onto Australia's AI ethics principle of contestability.

questions.stem: Packet sniffing is legitimate when used for:
options: Capturing device identifiers from shoppers' phones to measure store foot traffic
Recording which websites employees visit on the corporate network, without notice
Network diagnostics, intrusion detection, and lawful interception under warrant
Collecting credentials sent over an open Wi-Fi network, for security research
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are genuine grey areas that occur in practice, and both fail on notice and consent rather than on technical grounds. (D) fails regardless of intent. Defences against malicious sniffing: HTTPS/TLS everywhere, VPN, WPA3, MAC randomisation and network segmentation.

questions.stem: Intelligent systems relate to trolling in that they:
options: Are unrelated to it, since trolling is a social rather than a technical phenomenon
Detect it, though human moderators remain necessary for the final decision
Enable it, since recommendation systems reward outrage with reach
Both detect it (NLP toxicity classifiers, bot detection, moderation at scale) and enable it (bot amplification, outrage-rewarding recommendation, generative content)
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are each true and each only half the picture — which is exactly why they are tempting on a question that asks for the relationship. The dual role is the exam-worthy point. Relevant law: the eSafety Commissioner's powers under the Online Safety Act 2021.

questions.stem: Australia's under-16 social media restrictions, in force since 10 December 2025, were introduced by:
options: A new standalone Act, enforced by the ACCC
An amendment to the Privacy Act 1988, enforced by the OAIC
An amendment to the Online Safety Act 2021, enforced by the eSafety Commissioner
An industry code registered voluntarily by the platforms themselves
questions.explanation: Platforms must take reasonable steps to prevent under-16 accounts, with penalties up to $50 million. It forces the deployment of age-assurance systems — themselves intelligent systems, raising their own privacy questions.

questions.stem: Function creep in surveillance means:
options: A system being extended with new features beyond its original specification
A system gradually accumulating more data than it was originally designed to store
A system's accuracy degrading as the conditions it operates in change over time
A system deployed for one stated purpose being progressively used for others never consented to
questions.explanation: (A) is scope creep — a project management problem, not an ethical one, and the near-identical name is the trap. Number-plate cameras installed to find stolen vehicles, later used for parking enforcement and then for general movement tracking, is the classic pattern. Proportionality is the framework to apply.

questions.stem: The best framework for answering a surveillance ethics question is:
options: Security benefit versus privacy cost, proportionality, consent and transparency, accuracy and consequences of error, retention and access, function creep, accountability, chilling effects
Ownership, source, validation and risk, applied to the surveillance data collected
The four bias lenses, applied to the surveillance system's outputs
Confidentiality, integrity and availability, applied to the surveillance recordings
questions.explanation: (B), (C) and (D) are all genuine frameworks from elsewhere in this course, applied to the wrong question — a good reminder that naming a framework is not the same as naming the right one. Name it in your introduction, then work through it: it converts a vague question into a structured, markable answer.

questions.stem: Regarding AI and employment, the most defensible position is:
options: Net employment is unchanged, since displaced workers move into the roles AI creates
AI will eliminate substantially more roles than it creates, across every sector
Displacement is confined to routine manual and clerical work, leaving professional roles untouched
AI displaces some roles, creates others and transforms most, with gains distributed unevenly and transition speed the central policy problem
questions.explanation: (A) is the seductively balanced answer — the aggregate may hold, but it silently assumes the displaced worker and the new role are the same person, which is precisely the problem. Historically automation shifted rather than eliminated work, but the speed and cognitive reach of AI make this transition sharper. Roles most exposed: data entry, basic bookkeeping, call centres, routine QA.

questions.stem: "Working differently to complete the same task" is best illustrated by:
options: The human role being removed entirely once report production is fully automated
A human shifting from drafting reports to supervising, verifying and exception-handling AI-generated drafts
Report production being transferred to a lower-cost team in another country
A new role being created to build and maintain the report-generating model
questions.explanation: The other three are the neighbouring employment outcomes — displacement, offshoring and job creation. Here the goal is unchanged and only the method transforms, and the new skill demands are prompt and data literacy plus critical evaluation of AI output.

questions.stem: Australia's AI Ethics Principle of contestability requires that:
options: People affected by an AI decision can challenge it and seek review
The reasoning behind an AI decision can be explained to the person affected by it
An identifiable person or body is answerable for the AI system's outcomes
The system's outputs do not systematically disadvantage any particular group
questions.explanation: Every distractor is a different principle from the same set of eight: (B) transparency and explainability, (C) accountability, (D) fairness. The full eight: human/societal/environmental wellbeing, human-centred values, fairness, privacy protection and security, reliability and safety, transparency and explainability, contestability, accountability.

questions.stem: Australia's Guidance for AI Adoption (2025) consolidated the earlier voluntary standard into six practices, which are:
options: Governance and accountability, impact assessment, risk management, transparency, testing and monitoring, human oversight
Governance and accountability, impact assessment, risk management, contestability, testing and monitoring, human oversight
Governance and accountability, bias auditing, risk management, transparency, testing and monitoring, human oversight
Ownership, source, validation, risk, transparency, human oversight
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) each substitute one plausible term drawn from the AI ethics principles. These six are the practical checklist for an enterprise deploying AI, and the government has signalled legislated standards to follow.

questions.stem: From 2 August 2026, the EU AI Act's transparency obligations and general-purpose AI enforcement apply. Its relevance to an Australian enterprise is that:
options: It has no effect outside the EU, since Australian enterprises are governed by Australian law
An Australian enterprise whose AI system is placed on the EU market, or affects EU users, may fall within scope
It replaces the Privacy Act for any Australian enterprise deploying AI systems
It applies only to organisations with a physical presence in an EU member state
questions.explanation: Like GDPR, the AI Act has extraterritorial reach, which is what makes (A) and (D) wrong. Note that the high-risk (Annex III) obligations were deferred to 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus.

questions.stem: Automation bias is the tendency to:
options: Over-trust a system's output and under-scrutinise it, even when it is wrong
Prefer an automated process over a manual one regardless of the cost comparison
Reject an AI recommendation that conflicts with one's own prior judgement
Automate the tasks that are easiest rather than the tasks that are most valuable
questions.explanation: (C) is algorithm aversion, a genuine named effect running in exactly the opposite direction. Automation bias is why "human in the loop" is not automatically a safeguard — a human who rubber-stamps the machine adds no oversight, only the appearance of it.

questions.stem: The environmental argument regarding intelligent systems must consider:
options: E-waste from specialised hardware, which cannot be recycled through normal channels
The energy consumed during model training, which dominates the total lifecycle footprint
Energy and water for both training and inference, plus e-waste — set against efficiency gains in smart grids, logistics and precision agriculture
The carbon cost of data centres, which is offset entirely by renewable energy purchasing
questions.explanation: (B) is the widely repeated half-truth: training is a large one-off cost, but inference at scale — billions of queries — often exceeds it over a model's life. A balanced answer names both the footprint and the handprint, then makes a judgement.

questions.stem: Federated learning addresses which concern?
options: Latency — inference runs on the device rather than in the cloud
Accuracy — pooling data from many devices yields a much larger effective training set
Privacy — models are trained across devices without centralising raw personal data
Cost — training is distributed across devices the enterprise does not have to operate
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (D) are all genuine side effects of the architecture, which is what makes them tempting — but the reason federated learning exists is that only model updates leave the device, never the raw data. It is privacy by design applied to ML.

questions.stem: A deepfake used to impersonate a CEO authorising a payment is best categorised as:
options: An identity theft offence, adequately addressed by existing biometric protections
A failure of the payment system's authentication controls
A data quality problem, since the impersonation was not flagged as anomalous
Misuse of generative AI enabling social-engineering fraud, with accountability and verification implications
questions.explanation: (B) has a point — the payment process should not have relied on a voice — but it locates the problem in the victim's controls rather than in the capability that changed. Controls: out-of-band verification of payment instructions, callback procedures, and training that treats voice and video as no longer self-authenticating.

questions.stem: The digital divide in the context of intelligent systems means:
options: The separation between an enterprise's operational and its analytical data estates
The capability gap between enterprises that have adopted AI and those that have not
The difference between what a system can technically do and what its users believe it does
The benefits accrue to those with connectivity, devices and data literacy, while others are excluded or disadvantaged
questions.explanation: (B) describes a real and related phenomenon — sometimes called the AI divide — but at the level of organisations rather than people. The divide becomes acute when essential services (banking, government, health) assume digital access as the default.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to reduce unplanned equipment downtime. The best combination of technologies is:
options: A scheduled maintenance calendar generated from each machine's rated service interval
IoT vibration and temperature sensors + edge filtering + ML failure prediction + digital twin + automated work-order creation
A dashboard reporting historical downtime by machine, refreshed weekly
CCTV monitoring of the plant floor, with alerts raised by a human operator
questions.explanation: (A) is preventive maintenance — the near-miss worth naming, since it services on a schedule regardless of actual condition, replacing healthy parts and still missing early failures. (C) is descriptive analytics after the fact. Structure an extended response as need → technologies combined → how they work together → benefit → risk/limitation → evaluation.

questions.stem: A chatbot handles tier-1 support with escalation to humans. The most important design safeguard is:
options: Clear, low-friction escalation rules, so users reach a human when the system is out of its depth
A larger knowledge base, so that fewer queries fall outside the system's coverage
A confidence threshold below which the chatbot declines to answer at all
A disclosure at the start of the conversation that the user is talking to a machine
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) are both genuinely good practice, and (C) is closely related — but a threshold only helps if there is somewhere to escalate to, and low friction is what stops users abandoning the channel entirely. The narrow-domain failure mode — confidently wrong, with no path out — is what destroys trust in automated service.

questions.stem: A council deploys facial recognition in a public library. The strongest objection is:
options: The retention period applying to the biometric templates the system generates
The accuracy gap producing higher false-match rates for some demographic groups
Disproportionality — mass covert biometric collection in a low-risk setting, with chilling effects on access to a public service
The cost of installing and maintaining the camera and processing infrastructure
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are real objections — but both are answerable by improving the system, whereas proportionality asks the prior question of whether it should exist here at all. Apply the framework: is the intrusion justified by the risk, is there a less intrusive alternative, and what is the effect on people's willingness to use a public service?

questions.stem: A manufacturer's expert system for machine fault diagnosis stops matching reality after a plant upgrade. This illustrates:
options: Overfitting — the system was tuned too closely to the original plant's behaviour
Data drift — the distribution of sensor readings has shifted since the system was built
Knowledge base decay — expert systems cannot learn from experience and degrade as the domain changes
Brittleness — the system fails without recognising that it is operating outside its scope
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are machine learning concepts applied to a system that does no learning — an expert system has no training distribution to drift from and no parameters to overfit. (D) describes the symptom rather than the cause. Maintaining the knowledge base is an ongoing cost that is routinely under-budgeted, and a strong argument for hybrid systems that learn from operational data.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest justification for a hybrid rules-plus-ML system in a regulated industry?
options: The rules can be updated immediately while the ML component is being retrained
Running both and comparing their outputs catches errors that either would make alone
Rules provide auditable, legally defensible decisions where required, while ML handles noisy, high-dimensional inputs
The combination reduces the volume of training data the ML component requires
questions.explanation: (B) is a legitimate ensemble argument but is not specific to a regulated setting, which is what the stem asks about. Neuro-symbolic design keeps explainability where the law demands it, and statistical power where the problem demands it.

questions.stem: In an IoT deployment, a control loop requires a response within 20 ms. The correct architectural decision is:
options: Process in the cloud, using a low-latency 5G link to meet the deadline
Process at the edge, because round-trip latency to the cloud cannot reliably meet the deadline
Process at the edge for the decision, and in the cloud for the same decision as a cross-check
Process in the cloud, with the edge node caching the most recent decision as a fallback
questions.explanation: The word doing the work is reliably — (A) may meet 20 ms on a good day, and a control loop cannot depend on a good day. (C) and (D) add a cloud dependency to a deadline the cloud cannot guarantee. The cloud can still receive aggregates for analytics and model retraining.

questions.stem: A DSS recommends a course of action that managers consistently ignore. The correct evaluation is:
options: The DSS has failed — a technically accurate system nobody acts on delivers no value; investigate usability, explainability and trust
The DSS has succeeded, since its recommendations are accurate; the failure is an organisational one
The DSS needs more data, since managers evidently find its recommendations unconvincing
The recommendations should be made mandatory, removing the discretion to ignore them
questions.explanation: (B) is the sophisticated dodge, and (D) is the authoritarian one — neither asks why experienced managers disagree, which is usually the most informative signal available. Evaluate against accuracy, timeliness, usability, cost-benefit, and whether users trust and act on the output; adoption is a legitimate success criterion.

questions.stem: To assess a deployed DSS's output quality, the most rigorous method is:
options: Re-run the model on historical data and confirm that it reproduces the known outcomes
Survey the managers who use it on how accurate they find its recommendations
Graph predicted versus actual outcomes over time, compute an error measure, and test against a control or baseline
Audit the model's inputs against their source systems to confirm that they are correct
questions.explanation: (A) is backtesting, and it is genuinely useful — but a model tuned on that history will reproduce it, so it cannot distinguish learning from memorising. (D) validates the inputs, not the output. Comparing proposed versus actual with an explicit error measure, plus the business KPI the system was meant to move, is the evidence-based approach.

questions.stem: Verifying the data sources feeding a DSS should include all of the following except:
options: Cross-validating the data against an independent dataset
Accepting any dataset that supports the conclusion the enterprise already expects
Confirming the provenance and ownership of each source
Checking the collection methodology and the date of collection
questions.explanation: That is confirmation bias with a process wrapped around it. Also worth doing: check completeness and duplicates, assess publisher authority, confirm the licence, and document the audit trail so any output traces back to its inputs.

questions.stem: A retailer's recommendation engine increasingly shows customers only what they already buy. The concern is:
options: Class imbalance — the most popular products dominate the training data
Overfitting — the model has memorised individual customers rather than learning general patterns
Data drift — customer preferences have shifted since the model was last trained
Filter bubble / homogenisation — narrowing discovery and reinforcing existing behaviour
questions.explanation: All four are real ML phenomena, and (A) even contributes to the effect — but the concern named here is a feedback loop in which the system's own recommendations become tomorrow's training data. Mitigations: deliberate exploration in the ranking, diversity constraints, and transparency about why an item was recommended.

questions.stem: In a smart irrigation flowchart, deferring watering when rain is forecast within 6 hours demonstrates:
options: A feedback loop, since the outcome of each watering decision informs the next
A decision node combining sensor data with an external data source to avoid a wasteful action
Fuzzy logic, since "rain forecast" is a linguistic rather than a numeric variable
Backward chaining, since the system reasons back from the goal of avoiding waste
questions.explanation: Combining internal sensing with an external forecast API is what turns simple threshold automation into a genuinely intelligent decision. A forecast probability is numeric, which disposes of (C), and nothing here is fed back into the system's knowledge.

questions.stem: Autonomous vehicles raise which distinctive legal issue?
options: The privacy implications of continuously recording public streets
Ownership of the mapping and sensor data the vehicle generates as it drives
Allocation of liability between developer, deployer, operator and manufacturer when the system causes harm
Compliance with road rules drafted on the assumption of a human driver
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (D) are all genuine AV legal issues, but each has close analogues elsewhere — data ownership, street-level imagery and regulatory lag are all familiar problems. Liability for a decision no human made is the distinctive one. "The algorithm decided" is not a defence, and accountability structures must be settled before deployment rather than after the first incident.

questions.stem: An enterprise claims its AI recruitment tool is fair because it does not use gender as an input. The best critique is:
options: Proxy variables — school, suburb, career gaps, hobbies — can reconstruct the protected attribute, so removing the field does not remove the bias
Gender must be retained as an input, so that the model can correct for known differences between groups
Fairness cannot be assessed at all until a formal statistical definition of it has been chosen
The tool should be validated by an external auditor before any fairness claim is made
questions.explanation: This is "fairness through unawareness", and it does not work. Fairness must be tested on outcomes across groups, not asserted from the absence of an input field — and note the practical irony that you usually need the protected attribute recorded in order to run that test.

questions.stem: The best reason to keep a human in the loop for a consequential automated decision is:
options: It catches the errors the model makes, lifting overall accuracy above the model's own
It provides review, accountability and a contestability pathway for the affected person
It satisfies the transparency requirement, since a human can explain the decision afterwards
It allows the model to be retrained on the cases where the human disagreed with it
questions.explanation: (A) is the assumption automation bias destroys — a reviewer who defers to the machine catches nothing. (D) is a genuine benefit but a secondary one. Oversight is only real if the human has the information, the time, the authority and the incentive to disagree.

questions.stem: Which best demonstrates decomposition in designing a smart building system?
options: Recognising that temperature spikes reliably precede HVAC failures
Modelling each occupant as a heat source with a location and an output in watts
Splitting the system into sensing, pre-processing, decision logic, actuation, UI, logging and security subsystems
Writing the step-by-step control algorithm the HVAC subsystem will follow
questions.explanation: (B) is abstraction, (A) pattern recognition and (D) algorithm design — the other three computational thinking components, all correct descriptions of something and only one of them decomposition.

questions.stem: A supermarket's self-checkout uses computer vision to detect unscanned items. The most significant customer-facing risk is:
options: The cost of the additional hardware being passed through into shelf prices
Slower checkout, since every item must be visually verified before the sale completes
The privacy implications of recording customers at the checkout without explicit consent
False accusations arising from misclassification, damaging trust and potentially producing discriminatory outcomes
questions.explanation: (C) is a real concern and would score partial credit — but the stem asks what lands on the customer, and being wrongly stopped in front of other shoppers is a different order of harm. Accuracy failures in surveillance systems are not neutral errors; they arrive as accusations. Human review and a clear appeal path are essential controls.

questions.stem: The clearest evidence that an intelligent system meets an enterprise need is:
options: A favourable comparison against the equivalent systems deployed by competitors
The system's technical accuracy, measured on a held-out test set
High adoption, with staff using the system daily as part of their workflow
A measured improvement in the target business metric — downtime, fraud loss, conversion, cost per contact — against a pre-implementation baseline
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are both real evidence and both are proxies — an accurate system nobody uses and a popular system that changes nothing are equally common outcomes. Define the metric and the baseline before deployment, or evaluation becomes an argument rather than a measurement.

questions.stem: A digital twin of a water treatment plant is fed by sensors that have drifted out of calibration. The consequence is:
options: GIGO — the twin's recommendations become confidently wrong, and are trusted because the model looks sophisticated
The twin detects the discrepancy between its model and the readings, and raises an alarm
The twin's predictions gradually converge on the drifted readings, self-correcting over time
The twin stops producing output, since the readings fall outside its expected ranges
questions.explanation: (B) describes what a well-instrumented twin with explicit calibration monitoring would do — and the point is that this must be deliberately designed in, not assumed. Sensor calibration and data quality monitoring are part of the intelligent system, not a separate concern.

questions.stem: In an enterprise deploying an intelligent system, the most defensible order of activity is:
options: Select the technology → define the need it will address → pilot → measure → scale
Define the need → select the technology → scale across the enterprise → measure the outcome
Pilot a promising technology → identify the problems it solves → define success → scale
Define the need and success metric → design the combined solution → pilot → measure against baseline → scale or stop
questions.explanation: The critical element is "scale or stop" — (B) commits before measuring, and (A) and (C) are technology-led adoption, the most common and most expensive failure pattern in enterprise AI.

questions.stem: Which statement about IoT security is most accurate?
options: Constrained devices often ship with weak defaults and are patched infrequently, so device identity, encrypted transport, segmentation and OTA updates are essential
IoT devices present limited risk, because the devices themselves hold no valuable data
Encryption is unnecessary within a segmented local network that is unreachable from the internet
Physical access controls matter more than network controls, since most IoT attacks require device access
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are the two rationalisations that produce most IoT breaches — the value of a device is as a foothold, not as a data store, and "unreachable from the internet" survives exactly as long as nobody plugs anything in. The security layer spans device certificates, TLS/DTLS, VLAN segmentation, firewalls, OTA firmware updates and monitoring.

questions.stem: An enterprise uses an LLM to draft customer responses. The most important control is:
options: Human review before sending, plus logging, because the model can produce fluent but false or non-compliant content
Restricting the model to a knowledge base of approved company documents
Constraining output length, so that no unreviewed claim can be elaborated at length
Fine-tuning the model on the enterprise's own historical correspondence
questions.explanation: (B) and (D) are both real and worthwhile mitigations that reduce the rate of fabrication without eliminating it — a retrieval-grounded, fine-tuned model still confabulates, just more plausibly. Fluency is not accuracy, and in regulated communications an unreviewed generated statement is a compliance exposure.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest concluding judgement in an 8-mark question on intelligent systems in an enterprise?
options: "The system reduced average handling time by 34% and cost per contact by $2.10, while raising the escalation rate from 6% to 11% over the same period."

"On the criteria of measured efficiency gain and risk exposure, the system is justified — provided human oversight, bias auditing and a contestability pathway are maintained, without which the efficiency gain is achieved at an unacceptable accountability cost."
"The system was adopted because rising contact volume made the manual process the bottleneck, and because tier-1 queries were repetitive enough to be handled by rules."
"Compared with the manual process, the system is faster and cheaper per contact but less able to handle unusual cases, and it cannot explain its decisions to a customer who challenges one."
questions.explanation: A judgement, tied to stated criteria, with the conditions on which it depends made explicit. The others are each a different directive verb done well — (A) reports evidence, (C) explains, (D) compares — and none of them decides anything, which is precisely what "evaluate" and "discuss" require.

questions.stem: The feature that separates an intelligent system from ordinary automation is:
options: It processes larger volumes of data
It observes the outcome of its own decision and adjusts through a feedback loop
It is hosted in the cloud rather than on premises
It uses a relational database to store its rules
questions.explanation: A sprinkler on a timer is automation; one that measures soil moisture after watering and adapts its schedule is an intelligent system.

questions.stem: In the generic architecture, the knowledge/data store is updated by:
options: The input sensors directly
The feedback loop carrying measured outcomes back from the output stage
The user interface at each login
The actuator after each physical action
questions.explanation: Sensors feed processing, not the store. It is the measured result of a decision that updates what the system knows.

questions.stem: Which property of an intelligent agent describes acting on its own initiative rather than only responding?
options: Reactivity
Autonomy
Proactivity
Social ability
questions.explanation: Proactivity — Reactivity is responding to change, autonomy is acting without direct human control, and social ability is interacting with other agents — all four are examinable.

questions.stem: A system that decides using pre-coded IF-THEN rules and cannot adapt is:
options: A machine learning system
A knowledge-based expert system
A rule-based system
A decision support system
questions.explanation: An expert system also uses rules but adds an inference engine, certainty factors and an explanation facility — which is the closest distractor here.

questions.stem: The defining weakness of a rule-based system at scale is:
options: Rule explosion and conflicting rules, with no capacity to handle the unforeseen
It cannot be audited
It requires large labelled datasets
It cannot explain its decisions
questions.explanation: Rule-based systems are maximally explainable, so (B) and (D) invert their principal strength.

questions.stem: A DSS differs from a fully automated system because it:
options: Cannot access external data sources
Supports human judgement rather than replacing it
Uses only structured data
Operates without a user interface
questions.explanation: The clue in a stimulus is whether a human remains the decision-maker — a system that acts without a person is automation, not decision support.

questions.stem: Which DSS component holds the statistical, financial, optimisation and simulation models?
options: Data management
Dialogue management
Model management
Knowledge component
questions.explanation: Model management — Data management handles internal and external data, dialogue management is the user interface, and a knowledge component is the optional fourth.

questions.stem: "Auto-approve any refund under $50 where the order was delivered late" is:
options: A semi-structured decision requiring managerial judgement
A structured decision, fully automatable
An unstructured decision requiring executive input
Not a decision, since no human is involved
questions.explanation: The criteria are fully known and the rule is complete — humans monitor only. The presence of two conditions does not make it semi-structured.

questions.stem: The defining feature of a semi-structured decision is:
options: It has no rules at all
A specified finite set of instructions handles part of it, with judgement resolving the remainder
It is always made by executives
It cannot be supported by a computer system
questions.explanation: The contrast is with unstructured decisions, where the set of possible instructions is effectively infinite.

questions.stem: Moving up the decision pyramid from operational to strategic, the system's role shifts from:
options: Informing to deciding
Deciding to informing
Monitoring to controlling
Predicting to prescribing
questions.explanation: Alongside: ambiguity rises, data becomes more external and unstructured, frequency falls, and the consequence of a single error rises.

questions.stem: Which DSS feature answers "which combination of staff shifts minimises cost while meeting coverage rules"?
options: Optimisation modelling
Drill-down
Sensitivity analysis
Scenario comparison
questions.explanation: Optimisation searches for the best solution under constraints. Sensitivity analysis tests how fragile a result is to changed assumptions, which is the adjacent concept.

questions.stem: An airline's yield management system continuously adjusts fares. This is best classified as:
options: An unstructured strategic decision
A semi-structured decision requiring manager sign-off per fare
A structured decision automated within rules derived from demand models
Not a decision support application
questions.explanation: The pricing rules are fully specified, so the decision is automated at very high frequency — a textbook operational-level application.

questions.stem: Working memory in an expert system holds:
options: The permanent domain rules
The explanation of the last conclusion
The facts about the current case being reasoned over
The user's login credentials
questions.explanation: The knowledge base holds the permanent facts and rules; working memory is per-case and is cleared between consultations.

questions.stem: The knowledge acquisition subsystem exists to:
options: Collect facts about the current case from the user
Explain the reasoning chain to the user
Provide a route for updating the knowledge base as the domain changes
Select between forward and backward chaining
questions.explanation: (A) is the user interface's job during a consultation — the distinction between per-case facts and permanent knowledge is what is being tested.

questions.stem: A monitoring system receives continuous sensor readings and must determine what they imply. The appropriate inference strategy is:
options: Backward chaining, since it minimises questions
Ontology classification
Forward chaining, since it is data-driven
Fuzzy logic
questions.explanation: Data arrives without anyone being asked anything, and the system derives consequences as facts accumulate — the sensor rather than the doctor.

questions.stem: Backward chaining is preferred when:
options: Data is abundant and conclusions are numerous
The system must run without user interaction
There are few possible conclusions and gathering each fact is costly
The knowledge base contains no certainty factors
questions.explanation: It asks only for the facts needed to prove or disprove the current hypothesis — which is why it constantly queries the user.

questions.stem: Rules with certainty factors 1.0, 0.9 and 0.5 fire in a chain. The conclusion's confidence is:
questions.explanation: 0.45 — Multiply along the chain: 1.0 × 0.9 × 0.5. (D) is the trap of simply taking the weakest link, which is a different combination rule.

questions.stem: Two independent rules support the same conclusion with CF 0.5 and CF 0.4. Using CF = CF1 + CF2(1 − CF1), the combined value is:
questions.explanation: 0.70 — 0.5 + 0.4(1 − 0.5) = 0.5 + 0.2. (C) is the result of simply adding the two, which would allow confidence above 1 in other cases.

questions.stem: Confidence decays along a long inference chain. The appropriate system behaviour is to:
options: Report the conclusion with its confidence and request further evidence
Round the confidence up to the nearest 0.1 before reporting
Suppress the conclusion entirely below 0.5
Restart the consultation using forward chaining
questions.explanation: Graded confidence is the whole point of certainty factors — suppressing low-confidence conclusions (C) discards clinically or operationally useful information.

questions.stem: The explanation facility is what makes an expert system:
options: Faster than a human expert
Able to operate without a knowledge engineer
Able to learn from experience
Trustworthy and legally defensible, by tracing the rule chain behind a conclusion
questions.explanation: It answers "why are you asking this?" and "how did you reach that?" — a capability most modern black-box models lack.

questions.stem: Which activity falls outside the four syllabus applications of expert systems?
options: Diagnosis
Data warehousing
Scheduling and planning
Monitoring
questions.explanation: The fourth is process control. Interpretation, design/configuration and instruction are commonly added as further categories.

questions.stem: XCON, which configured DEC computer systems, is an example of expert systems used for:
options: Diagnosis
Scheduling
Monitoring
Design and configuration
questions.explanation: MYCIN is the canonical diagnosis example and PROSPECTOR the interpretation example — the three are commonly confused.

questions.stem: The knowledge acquisition bottleneck exists because:
options: Knowledge bases have limited storage capacity
Experts often cannot articulate knowledge they apply unconsciously
Inference engines process rules slowly
Domain experts are unwilling to participate
questions.explanation: Tacit knowledge is the barrier, and it is the main reason expert systems are slow and expensive to build — and a major driver of learning from data instead.

questions.stem: An expert system fails badly outside its domain and does not recognise the failure. The reason is:
options: Insufficient processing power
An inappropriate inference strategy
Corruption of the knowledge base
The absence of common sense and any representation of its own scope
questions.explanation: Brittleness combined with false confidence is the dangerous pairing — which is why explicit scope boundaries and human oversight are the standard controls.

questions.stem: Which factor did not drive the shift from purely rule-based to probabilistic systems?
options: Increased processing power
Standardisation of programming languages
Falling hardware costs
Greater data availability and access
questions.explanation: The syllabus factors are processing power, data availability and access, hardware costs, neural networks and webometrics.

questions.stem: Webometrics supports intelligent systems by:
options: Quantifying web content, links, usage and citations to infer relevance and authority statistically
Measuring server utilisation across a data centre
Compressing web pages for faster transmission
Encrypting search queries in transit
questions.explanation: Link analysis behind PageRank is the classic case — authority inferred from the structure of the web rather than hand-coded by an expert.

questions.stem: Which inference technique withdraws dependent conclusions when a premise is retracted?
options: Truth maintenance
Hypothetical reasoning
Heuristic knowledge
Fuzzy logic
questions.explanation: Truth maintenance — It records the justification for every derived fact, supporting non-monotonic reasoning where evidence is revised.

questions.stem: Exploring several competing diagnoses in parallel without committing to any is:
options: Hypothetical reasoning
Truth maintenance
Ontology classification
Fuzzy logic
questions.explanation: Used in medical differential diagnosis, financial scenario analysis and forensic reasoning — reasoning across possible worlds before choosing one.

questions.stem: A system handling the linguistic variable "slightly overloaded" uses:
options: Certainty factors
Heuristic pruning
Truth maintenance
Fuzzy logic
questions.explanation: Fuzzy logic — degrees of truth between 0 and 1 via membership functions. Certainty factors express confidence in a conclusion, not degrees of membership in a category.

questions.stem: Heuristic knowledge is used when:
options: An optimal solution must be guaranteed
Exhaustive search is impractical and a good-enough answer is needed quickly
The domain has no human experts
